content.summary_of_the_paper: The following work presents a TTS algorithm based on stable diffusion. Notably, its latent space is constrained to hold rich prosodic information via auxiliary objectives (self supervised tasks such as masked auto encoding). Factoring out non-prosodic information is achieved via standard augmentation-based disentanglement bottlenecks. The resulting prosody encoder, assumed to have most other information factored out, is then used to inform the low dimensional latent space in a latent diffusion architecture for the downstream TTS task.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Prosodic information is difficult to model, in large part due to F0 being unavailable in unvoiced segments of speech. Instead of imputing missing values and using F0 directly, they choose to create a latent space that is enforced to carry the same information as F0. This is certainly an interesting approach
- I appreciate some of the ablations in the latent diffusion experiments, specifically that they confirmed whether vector quantization had any qualitative benefit.

Weaknesses:
- While this work presents an interesting take on probabilistic modeling of prosodic information, there are some decent baselines available such as [1] to consider first.
- I'm not sure what to make of the MOS comparisons in Table 1 after having heard the samples provided on the author's website. On LJS, GradTTS appears to sound strictly better than everything -- even GT (voc). This is somewhat unusual. Maybe there's something wrong with the vocoder settings, or perhaps the wrong vocoder checkpoint is being used? On LibriTTS, the zero shot methods (GradTTS and yourtts) seem to have lost speaker fidelity (sounds like a different person, or mostly like a low grumble). Considering how clear GradTTS sounds on LJS, this is clearly a failure of the zero shot mechanism they employ, but I don't think it's reasonable to expect AMT raters to be able to separate these issues from the prosody and clarity evaluations.

Other comments and clarifications:
- I think the citation for the IEMOCAP work might be incorrect? I'm less familiar with this work, but I believe it should be [2]. 
- The choice of acronyms in Table 2 were very difficult to comprehend, as it's not clear what phrase they represent.


[1] Wang, Xin; Takaki, Shinji; Yamagishi, Junichi; King, Simon; Tokuda, Keiichi. A Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE) Autoregressive Neural F_0 Model for Statistical Parametric Speech Synthesis. IEEE/ACM TRANSACTIONS ON AUDIO, SPEECH, AND LANGUAGE PROCESSING 2018

[2] C. Busso, M. Bulut, C.C. Lee, A. Kazemzadeh, E. Mower, S. Kim, J.N. Chang, S. Lee, and S.S. Narayanan, "IEMOCAP: Interactive emotional dyadic motion capture database," Journal of Language Resources and Evaluation, vol. 42, no. 4, pp. 335-359, December 2008.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Most of the model/method description seems clear and should be mostly reproducible. There's definitely some novelty in latent prosodic modeling using an information bottleneck, but I think additional baselines are needed to demonstrate its necessity.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, interesting work. I think what's left to demonstrate is that existing approaches such as [1] (under strengths and weaknesses) do not suffice in probabilistic modeling of prosodic information, necessitating their latent approach. Furthermore, I do think there's some issues with the MOS evaluation as noted above that need to be resolved or clarified.

content.title: Response to Reviewer CUW9 (1/2)
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the constructive feedback and for considering our work as "appreciate the ablations" and "certainly an interesting approach". We understand that your concerns are mainly related to the paper's clarity and hope our response resolves your concerns fully.

**[About the baseline model]**

Thanks for the reviewer's suggestion, and we have included [1] as related work in the revised version of the paper. Wang et al. utilize the VQ-VAE framework to learn a latent code for the F0 contour of each linguistic unit, and adopts a second-stage model which maps from linguistic features to latent codes. Sharing a common weakness with baseline family, the local acoustic attributes extracted by the signal processing algorithm have inevitable information losses, which not only degrade the performance of the F0 prediction model but also hurt the optimization of TTS models. It's a pity that there is no publicly-available implementation of [1] and we fail to re-implement the performance reported in the original paper, and thus we cannot conduct the quantitative performance comparison with this work. 


**[About the MOS evaluation]**

Thanks for the reviewer's feedback and reminder that requests more exploration about our demo presentation and evaluation procedure. 
- For Grad-TTS, we used the publicly-available implementation at Github (https://github.com/huawei-noah/Speech-Backbones/tree/main/Grad-TTS). Following your observation, we noticed that the train set of the Grad-TTS LJSpeech checkpoint is overlapping with the testing list in our evaluation. That explains why the Grad-TTS sample sounds good. We should be careful next time not to provide misleading observations. As such, we re-train and re-evaluate the Grad-TTS model from scratch and update samples on the website. The updated samples fully match our conclusion. 
- For YourTTS, we used the publicly-available implementation at Github (https://github.com/coqui-ai/tts) and utilized the d-vector embedding from the reference utterance for multi-speaker synthesis. In most cases, the timbre of speech generated by YourTTS is consistent with the reference sample, while the degradation of speaker similarity could be observed clearly.

The evaluation of the TTS models is very challenging due to its subjective nature in the evaluation of the perceptual quality of generated speech. However, we use a sufficient number of metrics to measure the performance of our model, including the MCD and FFE objective evaluation. Our subjective evaluation tests are crowd-sourced and conducted by 25 native speakers via Amazon Mechanical Turk. In ablation studies, we further verify the effectiveness of several designs in Prosody-TTS by CMOS evaluation.

To address the reviewer's concern, we further include an AXY test to assess prosody expressiveness and naturalness across the testing set. For each sentence (A), the listeners are asked to choose a preferred one among the samples synthesized by baseline models (X) and proposed Prosody-TTS (Y), from which AXY preference rates are calculated. The scale ranges of 7-point are from ``X is much closer" to "Both are about the same distance" to "Y is much closer", and can naturally be mapped on the integers from -3 to 3. We explicitly instruct the raters to "focus on the naturalness of the prosody and style and ignore the differences of content, grammar, or audio quality.''. The results are presented in the following tables:

| Baseline   |    7-point score   |    X   |    Neutral   |   Y   |   
|----------|:-------------:|:-------------:|:-------------:|:-------------:|
|     FastSpeech 2      |  1.13$\pm$0.19     |   21\%    |   10\%  |  69\%      |
|     Meta-StyleSpeech       |    1.50$\pm$0.11     |   33\%    |    12\%   |    55\%  |
|        Glow-TTS        |   1.11$\pm$0.11   |  13\%  |    22\% |   65\%|
|   Grad-TTS          |     1.20$\pm$0.08      |   19\%    |     21\%    |   60\% |
|       YourTTS          |   1.42$\pm$0.10     |   28\%    |   13\%   |   59\% |


The side-by-side subjective test indicates that raters prefer our model synthesis against baselines in terms of prosody naturalness and expressiveness. Without relying on the paired transcriptions or local prosody attributes, Prosody-TTS generate speeches with natural prosody patterns and be superior to all baseline models, which covers diverse speaking styles (e.g., local rises and falls of the pitch and stress).

content.title: Response to Reviewer CUW9 (2/2)
content.comment:
**[About other comments and clarifications]**

Thanks for the reviewer's reminder. We have updated the citation of IEMOCAP dataset accordingly. Due to the page limitation in the manuscript, we adopt some abbreviations in Table 2 and attach detailed explanations in the caption.


**[About additional baselines]**

Thanks for the reviewer's suggestion for additional baseline comparison, we include the VITS model [3] and evaluate it in the LJSpeech dataset. The evaluation procedure stays consistent with the manuscript, and we present the results in the following tables:


|  Method   |    MOS-P     |   MOS-Q            |    MCD     |    FFE   |   
|----------|:-------------:|:-------------:|:-------------:|:-------------:|
|  VITS         | 4.02$\pm$0.07  | **4.05$\pm$0.06**  | **3.39**   | 0.42 |
|     Prosody-TTS  |    **4.10$\pm$0.06** |    4.03$\pm$0.05  |    3.52   |   **0.35**  |



In contrast to current two-stage models, VITS is designed to generate natural sound in an end-to-end manner. As VITS alleviates the error propagation between text-to-spectrogram and neural vocoding, it surpasses Prosody-TTS in terms of audio quality measured by MOS-Q and MCD. Regarding prosody naturalness (i.e., MOS-P and FFE), an apparent gap could be witnessed in VITS since it requests a paired corpus with transcriptions during training and constrains the distribution of learned representation. To conclude, Prosody-MAE significantly enhances prosody modeling by effectively capturing the prosodic style representation. Bridging the TTS conditions (i.e., textual features and target speaker) and Prosody-MAE features by latent diffusion, Prosody-TTS achieves high-fidelity speech synthesis with rich and natural prosody.


**[References]**

[1] Wang, Xin; Takaki, Shinji; Yamagishi, Junichi; King, Simon; Tokuda, Keiichi. A Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE) Autoregressive Neural F\_0 Model for Statistical Parametric Speech Synthesis. IEEE/ACM TRANSACTIONS ON AUDIO, SPEECH, AND LANGUAGE PROCESSING 2018

[2] Skerry-Ryan R J, Battenberg E, Xiao Y, et al. Towards end-to-end prosody transfer for expressive speech synthesis with tacotron. In Proc. ICML 2018.

[3] Kim J, Kong J, Son J. Conditional variational autoencoder with adversarial learning for end-to-end text-to-speech. In Proc. ICML 2021.

Again, we appreciate your valuable reviews and believe some misunderstandings are due to our clarity. In this rebuttal phase we will try to address them carefully, and we sincerely hope our response can fully resolve your concern.

Hi there! Thanks for the clarifications! They were helpful.

However, I went through the website samples and still identified some issues:

Notably, under "Diverse Multi-Speaker LibriTTS"

For Text: He spoke instead, in a light tone, as his pen still ran along.
The GT(VOC) sample does not match the text.

Furthemore, the prosody in the prosodyTTS samples of this section are nearly exactly that of ground truth. If these are reconstruction samples using prosody extracted from the original samples, that should be specified. This is especially noticeable in the sample:
Text: In a few days I had so far recovered my health that I could sit up all day, and walk out sometimes.
In that prosodyTTS is the only model that adds a pause between the words "health" and "that". 

All the durations for the prosodyTTS samples in that section were within .1s of the ground truth total duration, which is very unlikely unless the model has seen these during training or is performing resampling conditioned on ground truth prosody.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes a TTS model for expressive text-to-speech synthesis using self-supervised prosody pre-training and DDPM based generative method. The authors firstly train a self-supervised model to derive the prosodic representation and further build a TTS model using two diffusion modules. The first diffusion module learns the generation of prosodic representation while the second module learns the generation of mels-pectrograms. Experimental results on two public datasets confirms the effectiveness of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

The whole paper is overall well-written and well-organized.

The experimental results are overall promising.

Evaluation is thorough enough to support the arguments with in-depth ablation studies.

Weaknesses:

In section 3.4, "The refined sequences are fed into the vector quantization ...", what is the refined sequences? From figure 1b, it seems that the vector quantization layer receives the outputs from the latent diffusion (LD) module. However, the output of LD in the training phase is the Gaussian noise. There must be some misunderstanding - I thought the vector quantization is applied on the output of the prosody encoder.

Again in Figure 1b, the Diffusion Decoder receives the latent representation (which is of course of unknown distribution) and outputs the mel-spectrograms? So what is the prior distribution of the Diffusion Decoder?

In Appendix A, "we describe details of the linguistic encoder, prosody generator, and diffusion decoder", however, only the hyper-parameters are presented.

From my point of view, it is a weird design choice to add a quantization layer after a powerful generative module. The goal of the generative module is to produce the output with as much detail as possible while the goal of a quantization layer is to preserve important features.

Multi-speaker synthesis setting is not presented, however, the experimental results on a multi-speaker dataset is presented.

No comparison over the computational cost nor inference speed is presented. It is of particular interest because DDPM models often suffer from higher computational cost.

According to the authors' design choice, the length predictor (or the duration predictor) is independent of the prosody information, can you give some explanations?

I will re-evaluate the score based on the authors' response.

content.title: Response to Reviewer y492 (1/2)
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the constructive feedback and for considering our work as "overall promising" and "evaluation is thorough". We understand that your concerns are mainly related to the paper's clarity and hope our response resolves your concerns fully.


**[About the information flow in vector quantification layer]**

Thanks for the reviewer's feedback that requests more clarification to resolve the misunderstanding on the vector quantification (VQ) layer.

"refined sequence" represents the prosodic representation for quantification, which comes from different origins respectively in the training or inference stages: 
- When training the TTS model, the VQ layer receives the clean features derived from the prosody encoder in Prosody-MAE instead of the noisy output by forward diffusion. 
- During the inference stage, the VQ layer receives the prosodic representation via LDM's backward latent denoising, which bridges the TTS conditions (i.e., textual features and target speaker) and prosody features.

**[About the information flow in diffusion decoder]**

Thanks for the reviewer's feedback that requests more explanations about the information flow in the diffusion decoder. 

The diffusion decoder receives the latent representation as condition signals and outputs the mel-spectrograms. Following the common assumption in DDPMs [1], our diffusion decoder inherently samples from the Gaussian prior distribution. Conditioning on the textual hidden representation, the diffusion decoder approximates the target distribution by iterative refinement, where a guarantee of high sample quality requires multiple de-noising steps.

**[About the detailed information in appendix]**

Thanks for the reviewer's suggestion. We have revised the instance and attached more information on prosody encoder and diffusion mechanism in the new version of the paper.

**[About the design of vector quantification layer]**

Thanks for the reviewer's feedback that requests more clarification on the design of a vector quantification layer. 

It has been reported [2] that due to the expressiveness of the generative diffusion model, the produced latent spaces could be highly variant and diverse. To avoid instability, we impose a vector quantization (VQ) layer after the latent diffusion module for regularization: 1) It ensures that prosodic codes are produced inside the look-up table, avoiding that out-of-domain continuous distribution is sampled which hurts performance; and 2) The default size of the code book in the VQ layer is set to 1000, and the large table prevents the degradation of expressiveness and diversity after quantification.

**[About the multi-speaker setting]**

In response to the reviewer's question, we had attached the multi-speaker dataset setup in Section 4.1.2 in the original manuscript. For the multi-speaker scenario, we utilize the 300-hour LibriTTS dataset derived from LibriSpeech. We include a d-vector speaker embedding to capture the voice characteristic of each speaker following the common practice.



**[About the computational cost]**

Thanks for the reviewer's feedback that requests more explanation on the computational cost. As DDPMs [1] are gradient-based models, a guarantee of high sample quality typically comes at the cost of hundreds to thousands of de-noising steps. Prosody-TTS adopts generative diffusion models for high-quality synthesis, and thus it inherently requires multiple iterative refinement for better results. 

Though the denoising sampling could be accelerated by several techniques (e.g., scheduler (DDIM [3], PNDM [4]), or training diagram (Progressive Distill [5])), it is beyond our focus in this paper, and thus we leave it for future work.

**[About the duration module]**

Thanks for the reviewer's feedback that requests more explanation about our design. In Prosody-TTS, the duration predictor is independent of the prosody information. 

Though the duration predictor can include textual and prosody-MAE features as joint input to improve rhythm modeling, we inherit the original architecture from the baselines [6-10] and leave it unchanged for a more fair comparison. As such, we attribute the success of Prosody-TTS to better capturing and producing natural prosody patterns (e.g., local rises and falls of the pitch and stress).

content.title: Reply to the response
content.comment:
I would like to sincerely thank the authors for the detailed response. The authors explained more details about the diffusion decoder and VQ layer. I appreciate these responses, but I tend to keep the current score due to the following concerns:

1. The information flow in Figure 1b is clearly wrong based on the authors' responses. I'm glad to see that the VQ layer receives the features derived from the prosody encoder during the training. But unfortunately, there has been no corrections made in Figure 1b and 1c. 

2. The MOS results are not convincing. The audios from baselines and Prosody-TTS in the demo page are noisy. The authors didn't provide samples of YourTTS and VITS. I synthesized and compared those samples using the official implementation and pre-trained weights. In my subjective evaluation, it is observed that VITS and YourTTS clearly synthesize better quality audio.

3. It is hard to justify the use of the method in practice. Considering this method requires significantly large computational cost to generate the expressive audio examples, it is less competitive when compared with SOTA models such as VITS. 

I therefore keep my score unchanged.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2778 by Reviewer wALL

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: Proposes a TTS model consisting of a prosody encoder that is pre-trained in a self-supervised manner, followed by a FastSpeech-like model consisting of a latent diffusion model for sampling a prosodic latent variable followed by a diffusion decoder to predict spectrograms, and a HifiGAN vocoder.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths

* Allows pre-training a “prosody” encoder on untranscribed speech datasets, increasing the data quantity and diversity that can be used for training TTS. This encoder learns a time-domain encoding of prosody, hopefully invariant to speaker and lexical content.

# Weaknesses

* Duration is a major component of prosody, yet is not handled by the latent diffusion model that is in charge of modeling “prosody”. This is the biggest weakness of the method, as it will never overcome the unimodal prediction problems the authors describe when durations are predicted with conditional independence assumptions and an L1 loss.
* Does not compare to VITS, a successor to Glow-TTS which has strong LJSpeech performance and does not suffer as badly from the average / flat prosody issues that other models like FastSpech does: https://jaywalnut310.github.io/vits-demo/index.html
* The authors compare across models with highly similar MOS using the MOS numbers instead of running a CMOS or MUSHRA eval. This makes it difficult to believe the results are not within the noise.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The manuscript could use work.
* Improve clarity and organization of argument.
* Tone down unnecessary bombast and over-claiming.
* Improve precision of language -- e.g. it's not clear how we could say that a model suffers from "sub-optimal modeling".

My recommendations for improvements, per section, are as follows:

* 1: “Prosody capturing and modeling” – this section could use work. 
  * “Local prosody ground truth” is referring to the FastSpeech-style approach of solving the one-to-many mapping problem by reducing the “many” part. I strongly agree with your point that the DSP-based methods for e.g. pitch extraction can fail, and badly – so this route is best to be avoided.
  * This section is missing the line of work explicitly representing prosody with latent variables (e.g. fine grained, global, or hierarchical) as a method of solving the one-to-many problem. VITS is not doing this, as it represents the actual output variable X in a variational manner. Variational inference is not the only way to do this.  
  * “they generally request paired corpus with transcriptions, and thus the distribution of learned representation has been constrained to the TTS training data.” I suggest striking this sentence as it is not true. The only type of model that would preclude pre-training on untranscribed data would be latent variables represented on the text-side (e.g. phoneme or grapheme level). And even here, unsupervised TTS methods or TTS/ASR-in-one-model methods are able to do this.
* 1: “Prosody producing and sampling” – the text of this paragraph describes the oversmoothing problem in TTS, yet the title talks about prosody and also over-smoothing in latent space. I’m very confused by this section. 
  * I think you are describing two things: over-smoothing caused by unimodal and conditional independence assumptions made implicitly by the use of MSE or MAE losses for e.g. spectrogram prediction.
  * Something about prosody latent spaces and L1/L2 losses in that space. Please clarify.
* 2.1: “represents a success in modeling the variational attributes” – I think you mean “variation”, not “variational”.
* “However, these methods rely on text transcriptions or local prosody ground truth for regularization, leading sub-optimal modeling or distribution collapse.”
  * What is “distribution collapse” and which TTS models suffer from it? (and how do you show that?).
  * Why does using text transcriptions or frame-level acoustic features lead to “sub-optimal modeling”?
* 3.1: “The self-supervised training manner ensures Prosody-MAE covers diverse speaking styles;“
  * This is not an inherently true statement. Obviously it is only the case if you pre-train it on datasets containing diverse speaking styles.
* 3.2: The List of (1) (2) (3) is difficult to parse. Make it a bulleted list?
* 3.2: “Instead of considering the time-align masking operation, the hierarchal masking learns both the temporal and frequency structure.”
  * What is hierarchical masking?
* 3.2: “The model could capture the prosodic representation more efficiency by residual”: Incomplete sentence?
* 3.2: “style (i.e. pitch and energy)” 
  * style is not the same thing as energy and pitch and I would be loathe to let this synecdoche proliferate further. 
  * Perhaps use the term “frame-level acoustic features”. Please correct throughout the manuscript. 


* Figure 1: “Vector Quantification” -> “Vector Quantization”
* 3.3: “Extremely faithful”, “strongly matching” – The verbiage is over the top. I suggest quantifying the faithfulness of the reconstruction. “Show don’t tell” is more effective. Further, this text is coming before we’ve seen any experiment sections in your manuscript!
* 3.3: The text does not describe the sampling procedure for latent representations.
* 3.3: Please describe the connection between the prosody encoder and latent diffusion model in more detail. Is the output of the prosody encoder patch embeddings? How do these connect to the latent diffusion model? Is the latent diffusion model producing a single global embedding? A sequence of embeddings (in the time domain? At the phoneme level?). The text does not specify, or I may have missed it.
* 3.4: “Arbitarily high variance latent spaces” – I think you mean high dimensional? Even a 1D latent space can have high variance.
* 3.4: Equation 3: $p$ is not defined. Replace $L_r$ with $L_c$ to match 3.5.1?
* 3.5.1 “discriminative gradient” – what is this?  “Commit loss” -> “commitment loss”
* Table 2: Please be more specific about what it means to ablate the “carefully-crafted information flow”.
* Samples page: 
  * what is “Variational Inference” in the ablation study?
  * The LibriTTS audio sample are surprisingly bad for almost all methods. Are we sure these are strong enough baselines?
* 4.2: “Without relying on text transcriptions our model is demonstrated to cover diverse speaking styles and avoid sub-optimal predictions.” 
  * I disagree that the experiments demonstrate this. 
  * The datasets used for evaluation are not diverse – LJSpeech is highly neutral / boring prosodically. 
  * If you intend to show prosodic diversity -- provide some demos that show the different prosodic trajectories your model is able to emit for the same prosodically ambiguous sentence. Or present metrics that attempt to quantify the diversity of trajectories your model emits. 
  * How would we show that a model “avoids sub-optimal predictions”? 
  * Unless I have grossly misunderstood your method, your model is trained with the text of the TTS datasets. I believe you mean that your Prosody-MAE pre-training phase does not make use of text transcriptions – but it’s inaccurate to say your model doesn’t rely on text transcriptions.
* 4.3: “Similar to the MAE paper demonstrated for the visual domain” – please add a citation.
* 4.3: Comparison with other state-of-the-art: “We compare our proposed Prosody-MAE to [wav2vec2, hubert, robust hubert, mae-ast]”. Where are the results for these experiments? What metrics did you use to evaluate them? Downstream performance on TTS? 
* 4.4: “with the regression based style predictor”
  * Citation? Is this FastSpeech’s default f0/energy predictor?
* Table 1: Mention that YourTTS is a grapheme-based model, and so this comparison is not apples-to-apples.
* Please add some samples from the model that aren’t in the LJSpeech or LibriTTS corpora so we can hear how it generalizes to unseen text that isn't in the LJSpeech / Librivox style.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I appreciate the author’s work and found this an interesting read. I think the role of pre-training in TTS is under-explored and like the direction towards being able to use untranscribed datasets.

However, I had many issues with the manuscript in its current form. At a high level, I think the approach inherits weaknesses of FastSpeech (the duration prediction for one) which significantly limits the ability of the prosody encoder to improve the bad decisions made in the duration predictor. The latent diffusion approach seems to be related to prosody latent variable methods, yet the authors do not compare to any methods that use prosody latent variables. It feels as though the latent diffusion model could greatly improve the sampling process for prosody latent variables but this is not demonstrated by the authors e.g. by training on a prosodically diverse dataset and showing the diversity of prosodic samples you can draw for the same text. The authors claim multiple times their approach produces diverse samples but do not attempt to demonstrate this.

The demo page makes me think the baselines are very weak. I would like to see stronger LJSpeech baselines, such as VITS (which reports a higher MOS on LJ). Further – I think CMOS or MUSHRA are the preferred methods of comparing highly similar systems. MOS is not sensitive enough for a job where many TTS systems are scoring in the ~4 range.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Response to Reviewer wALL (1/5)
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the constructive feedback and for considering our work as "increasing data quantity and diversity" and "like the direction towards being able to use untranscribed datasets". We understand that your concerns are mainly related to the paper's clarity, and hope our response resolves your concerns fully.

Before addressing your concerns, we would like to clarify the focus and contributions of this paper first. 
- We propose prosody-MAE, a self-supervised model that captures prosody-related variations from speech without relying on transcriptions. With several novel designs (i.e., carefully-crafted information flow, mask strategy, and multi-task learning), prosody-MAE is expected to explicitly learn more content and speaker agnostic information that composes a natural speech. On the IEMOCAP benchmark, we demonstrated a SOTA performance of Prosody-MAE in amplifying prosodic information and normalizing speaker and content variabilities. 
- To incorporate Prosody-MAE into the text-to-speech (TTS) framework, we investigate a latent diffusion model which bridges the TTS conditions (i.e., textual features and target speaker) and prosody-MAE representations. With the novel and powerful generative model, we are able to generate speech with largely improved prosody naturalness and diversity. 
- Jointly with Prosody-MAE as the SSL prosodic patterns learner and a diffusion model as a sampler, our developed prosody-TTS framework no longer requires local prosodic attributes that cause inevitable information losses. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed framework surpasses the competing models in terms of audio quality and prosody naturalness.




In the next sections, we will address your concerns accordingly, and we hope our response fully resolves your concern.  

**[About the duration model]**

Thanks for the reviewer's feedback that requests more clarification about our design in this work. We agree with the reviewer that rhythm is a major component of prosody. In practice, however, baseline models demonstrate their superiority in expressive speech synthesis with inherited duration prediction (regression duration predictor [10,11,14] or stochastic duration predictor[12,13]). For a fair comparison, we inherit the duration module and leave it unchanged. 

Without improving rhythm modeling at the same time (using textual and Prosody-MAE features as joint input), it's appropriate and reasonable to attribute the success of Prosody-TTS to better capturing and producing natural prosody patterns (e.g., local rises and falls of the pitch and stress). 

For a better understanding of rhythm in comprising prosody in the LJSpeech benchmark, we utilize the oracle duration derived by forced alignment in our backbone (FastSpeech 2) for comparison. The MOS-P evaluation procedure stays consistent with the manuscript, where we explicitly instruct the raters to "focus on the naturalness of the prosody and style and ignore the differences of content, grammar, or audio quality."

|  Method  |      MOS-P               |    MCD    |    FFE    |   
|----------|:-------------:|:-------------:|:-------------:|
|   Backbone   |   3.92$\pm$0.07  |  3.88   |  0.43  | 
 |  Backbone + GT duration   |  3.97$\pm$0.06     |  3.79     |  0.40    | 
|  Prosody-TTS   |  4.10$\pm$0.06   |  3.52   |  0.35 |  



As illustrated in Table, the optimized rhythm leads to the MOS-P gain with a score of 0.05 compared to the original backbone, while Prosody-TTS still demonstrates the leading performance. The perfect duration may still suffer some prosody problems, indicating the importance and necessity of explicitly adding a prosody branch for expressive TTS. In fact, with prosody-MAE, we can use the learned prosody representation to improve the baseline duration predictor, and thus it acknowledges the reviewer's comments but also shows the importance of Prosody-MAE.

content.title: Response to Reviewer wALL (2/5)
content.comment:
**[About comparison to VITS]**

In response to the reviewer's question, we have adopted YourTTS as one of our baseline models, which is built upon VITS and demonstrate to achieve the SOTA results in voice similarity and audio quality. It includes several modifications for predicting a latent variable z instead of the raw waveform, which is used as input to the HIFI-GAN vocoder generator for speech generation.

Thanks for the reviewer's suggestion. We further include the VITS model [2] for comparison in the LJSpeech dataset. The evaluation procedure stays consistent with the manuscript, and we present the results in the following tables:

|  Method   |    MOS-P     |   MOS-Q            |    MCD     |    FFE   |   
|----------|:-------------:|:-------------:|:-------------:|:-------------:|
|  VITS         | 4.02$\pm$0.07  | **4.05$\pm$0.06**  | **3.39**   | 0.42 |
|     Prosody-TTS  |    **4.10$\pm$0.06** |    4.03$\pm$0.05  |    3.52   |   **0.35**  |


In contrast to current two-stage models, VITS is designed to generate natural sound in an end-to-end manner. As VITS alleviates the error propagation between text-to-spectrogram and neural vocoding, it surpasses Prosody-TTS in terms of audio quality measured by MOS-Q and MCD. Regarding prosody naturalness (i.e., MOS-P and FFE), an apparent gap could be witnessed in VITS since it requests a paired corpus with transcriptions during training and constrains the distribution of learned representation. To conclude, Prosody-MAE significantly enhances prosody modeling by effectively capturing the prosodic style representation. Bridging the TTS conditions (i.e., textual features and target speaker) and Prosody-MAE features by latent diffusion, Prosody-TTS achieves high-fidelity speech synthesis with rich and natural prosody.

**[About the subjective evaluation]**

Thanks for the reviewer's feedback that requests more explanations about our evaluation. The evaluation of the TTS models is very challenging due to its subjective nature in the evaluation of the perceptual quality of generated speech. However, we use a sufficient number of metrics to measure the performance of our model, including the MCD and FFE objective evaluation. Our subjective evaluation tests are crowd-sourced and conducted by 25 native speakers via Amazon Mechanical Turk. In ablation studies, we further verify the effectiveness of several designs in Prosody-TTS by CMOS evaluation.

Thanks for the reviewer's suggestion. Following previous literature [3], we randomly choose $20$ reference signals from the testing set and include an AXY test to assess the prosody expressiveness and naturalness. For each sentence (A), the listeners are asked to choose a preferred one among the samples synthesized by baseline models (X) and proposed Prosody-TTS (Y), from which AXY preference rates are calculated. The scale ranges of 7-point are from "X is much closer" to"Both are about the same distance" to "Y is much closer", and can naturally be mapped on the integers from -3 to 3. We present results in the following tables:

| Baseline   |    7-point score   |    X   |    Neutral   |   Y   |   
|----------|:-------------:|:-------------:|:-------------:|:-------------:|
|     FastSpeech 2      |  1.13$\pm$0.19     |   21\%    |   10\%  |  69\%      |
|     Meta-StyleSpeech       |    1.50$\pm$0.11     |   33\%    |    12\%   |    55\%  |
|        Glow-TTS        |   1.11$\pm$0.11   |  13\%  |    22\% |   65\%|
|   Grad-TTS          |     1.20$\pm$0.08      |   19\%    |     21\%    |   60\% |
|       YourTTS          |   1.42$\pm$0.10     |   28\%    |   13\%   |   59\% |

    
The side-by-side subjective test indicates that raters prefer our model synthesis against baselines in terms of prosody naturalness and expressiveness. Without relying on text transcriptions or local prosody attributes, Prosody-TTS covers diverse speaking styles superior to all baseline models and avoid sub-optimal predictions. 

**[About clarity and reproducibility]**

Thanks for the reviewer's suggestion. We have refined the mentioned instance accordingly and included the reproducibility statement in Appendix I in the revised version of the paper.

content.title: Response to Reviewer wALL (3/5): Regarding the minor concerns and suggestions
content.comment:
We appreciate the reviewer's detailed reviews and understand that your concerns are mainly related to the paper’s clarity. In this rebuttal phase, we will try to address these minor concerns and suggestions below carefully:


> **Q1**: This section is missing the line of work explicitly representing prosody with latent variables

**A1:** We have included a line of works that utilize conditional variational auto-encoder and sample hierarchical prosody features as related works in Section 1.

> **Q2**: The only type of model that would preclude pre-training on untranscribed data would be latent variables represented on the text side.

**A2:** In response to the reviewer's question, the aforementioned methods rely on textual representation as a conditional signal for capturing the prosody distribution, while the requirement of a transcript dataset hurts model generalization. In contrast, we propose to effectively learn the prosodic distribution given speech samples without relying on pre-trained TTS models or text transcriptions.

> **Q3**: the text of this paragraph describes the over-smoothing problem in TTS, yet the title talks about prosody and also over-smoothing in latent space

**A3:** Thanks for the reviewer's feedback that requests more clarification on over-smoothing predictions. It has been known that simple MSE-based reconstruction losses assume that data points are independent of each other and follow a unimodal distribution. As such, the highly multimodal latent representation cannot be well modeled by the L1 or L2 losses, which presents great challenges in prosody modeling and causes over-smoothed (blurred) predictions. In contrast, we utilize generative diffusion models to sample the diverse codes within the learned latent space. Specifically, it optimizes the evidence lower bound (ELBO) and sample results by iterative refinement, and thus we expect our model to exhibit better diversity and prevent the model from learning the collapsed distribution.



> **Q4**: I think you mean “variation”, not “variational”.

**A4:** Thanks for the reviewer's suggestion and reminder. We have updated the presentation accordingly. 

> **Q5**: What is “distribution collapse” and which TTS models suffer from it? (and how do you show that?).

**A5:** Thanks for the reviewer's suggestion. We agree with the reviewer that the diversity of prosodic distribution is not fully justified. As distribution coverage of speech samples [5] could be measured with metrics such as the number of Statistically-Different Bins (NDB) and Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD), we evaluate by 1) clustering the training data into several clusters, and 2) measuring how well the generated samples fit into those clusters. For easy comparison, the results are presented in the following table. 



| Method   |    NDB (LJSpeech)    |   JS (LJSpeech)     |   NDB (LibriTTS)    | JS (LibriTTS)     |   
|----------|:-------------:|:-------------:|:-------------:|:-------------:|
|     GT                       |  /          |  /         |   /      |  /        |
|      GT(voc.)             |  19        |   0.02  |   41	|  0.01  |
|      FastSpeech 2    |    45	|   0.05 |   74	|   0.04 |
|  Meta-StyleSpeech |    41	|   0.07 |   58	|   **0.01** |
|      Glow-TTS          |    34	|  0.03 |   61	|   0.03 |
|      Grad-TTS          |    49	|   0.13 |   71	|   0.05 |
|   YourTTS               |    47	|   0.08 |   73	|   0.06 | 
|  Prosody-TTS        |   **30**	|   **0.03**  |   **52**	|   **0.01** |  


In terms of sample diversity, we can see that Prosody-TTS scores the superior NDB with scores of $30$ (LJSpeech) and $52$ (LibriTTS), demonstrating that Prosody-TTS surpasses the baseline models in generating samples with diverse prosody patterns (e.g., local rises and falls of the pitch and stress). Informally, by breaking the generation process into several conditional diffusion steps, generative latent diffusion prevents TTS from learning collapsed prosodic distribution. In contrast, most baseline models learn a mean distribution over their input data which leads to dull speech synthesis with similar patterns.



> **Q6**: Why does using text transcriptions or frame-level acoustic features lead to “sub-optimal modeling”.

**A6:** The aforementioned methods rely on a paired corpus with transcriptions and constrain the learned representation to the paired TTS data, leading to a sub-optimal solution [6] that overfits the TTS training data and explicit poor generalization.


> **Q7**: Obviously it is only the case if you pre-train it on datasets containing diverse speaking styles.

**A7:** In the pre-training stage, we utilize the commonly-used LibriSpeech dataset with labels discarded. Librispeech provides 960 hours of audiobook data in English, read by over 1,000 speakers. It ensures the Prosody-MAE covers various speaking styles and distributions in diverse speech corpora.

display_title: Response to Reviewer wALL (4/5): Regarding the minor concerns and suggestions

content.title: Response to Reviewer wALL (4/5): Regarding the minor concerns and suggestions
content.comment:
> **Q8**: The List of (1) (2) (3) is difficult to parse. Make it a bulleted list?

**A8:** Thanks for the reviewer's suggestion and reminder. We have updated the presentation accordingly. 


> **Q9**: 3.2: What is hierarchical masking?

**A9:** Different from masking to time steps in continuous waveforms as in previous works [8,9], we mask patches in both frequency channels and time steps which assist in learning both the temporal and frequency structure. Thus we expect the model to exhibit better abilities in learning style attributes.

> **Q10**: The model could capture the prosodic representation more efficiency by residual: Incomplete sentence?

**A10:** Thanks for the reviewer's suggestion and reminder. We have updated the presentation accordingly. 

> **Q11**: style is not the same thing as energy and pitch and I would be loathe to let this synecdoche proliferate further.

**A11:** Thanks for the reviewer's feedback that requests more clarification to resolve the misunderstanding. In section 3.2, we utilize ``style classification" to denote the auxiliary pitch and energy objective in multi-task learning, which guarantees the model focus on modeling and capturing the speaking style. 

> **Q12**: I suggest quantifying the faithfulness of the reconstruction.

**A12:** In response to the reviewer, we have attached the quantitative evaluation in Section 4.4 in the original manuscript. Replacing the latent diffusion model with the regression-based style predictor results in decreased prosody naturalness and expressiveness with scores of 0.11 CMOS-P and 0.04 CMOS-P. To conclude, the latent diffusion model is efficiently trained by optimizing ELBO without adversarial feedback, and thus we expect our model to exhibit better diversity and prevent generating dull samples with mean prosodic distribution.


> **Q13**: The text does not describe the sampling procedure for latent representations.

**A13:** We include the sampling procedure in Section 3.5.2 in the original manuscript and update the diagram in Figure 3 in Appendix A.2. Specifically, the latent diffusion model first randomly samples a latent noise, and iteratively denoises it to produce a new prosodic representation in latent space conditioning on linguistic information.

> **Q14**: Please describe the connection between the prosody encoder and latent diffusion model in more detail. Is the output of the prosody encoder patch embeddings? How do these connect to the latent diffusion model? Is the latent diffusion model producing a single global embedding? A sequence of embeddings (in the time domain? At the phoneme level?). The text does not specify, or I may have missed it.

**A14:** The coverage Prosody-MAE derives patch-level latent representations for training the TTS model, which is a frame-level sequence of fine-grained embedding. A latent diffusion model (LDM) is explored to bridge TTS inputs (i.e., textual input and target speaker) and the prosody representation: 1) During training, the LDM receives representation derived from Prosody-MAE and optimizes the ELBO loss via the forward diffusion; 2) During inference, the LDM samples from Gaussian distribution and produces the prosodic representation via backward denoising, which bridges the TTS conditions and latent representation to better model the prosody patterns.


> **Q15**:  “Arbitarily high variance latent spaces” – I think you mean high dimensional? Even a 1D latent space can have high variance.


**A15:** Thanks for the reviewer's feedback that requests more clarification on the high variance latent spaces. It has been reported [15] that due to the expressiveness of the generative diffusion model, the produced latent spaces could be highly variant and diverse. To avoid instability, we impose a vector quantization (VQ) layer after the latent diffusion module for regularization. Specifically, it prevents the train-and-inference mismatch by constraining the prosody representations sampled inside the look-up table.

> **Q16**: About equation and abbreviations

**A16:** Thanks for the reviewer's reminder. We have updated the equation and abbreviations in the revised version of the paper.



> **Q17**: Please be more specific about what it means to ablate the “carefully-crafted information flow”.

**A17:** We decompose the speech variants into linguistic content, speaker, and prosody variations in section 3.2.1. By introducing pre-trained speech encoders to restrict the information flow, the prosody encoder could capture the prosodic representation more efficiently as residual attributes.

content.title: Response to Reviewer wALL (5/5): Regarding the minor concerns and suggestions
content.comment:
> **Q18**: what is “Variational Inference” in the ablation study?

**A18:** In ablation studies, we compare different prosody modeling techniques in TTS models to check which demonstrates better performance. Specifically, we use ``Variational Inference" to denote the line of methods that utilize conditional variational auto-encoder and sample the global, local, or hierarchical prosody features from a conditional prior distribution.

> **Q19**: The LJSpeech used for evaluation are not diverse

**A19:** Following previous practice [11,12] in expressive text-to-speech, we additionally utilize the 300-hour multi-speaker LibriTTS dataset with diverse acoustic attributes for a clear comparison. 


> **Q20**: “Similar to the MAE paper demonstrated for the visual domain” – please add a citation.

**A20:** Thanks for the reviewer's reminder. We have updated the citation in the revised version of the paper.

> **Q21**: Comparison with other state-of-the-art: “We compare our proposed Prosody-MAE to [wav2vec2, hubert, robust hubert, mae-ast]”. Where are the results for these experiments? What metrics did you use to evaluate them? Downstream performance on TTS?

**A21:** We compare our proposed Prosody-MAE with several speech SSL models and present the results in Table 2. Different from these baselines which capture linguistic content and derive prosody-agnostic representation, Prosody-MAE focuses on learning prosody patterns and thus we introduce style-aware downstream challenges (i.e., frame-level pitch and energy recognition) on the commonly-used dataset IEMOCAP for evaluation. Specifically, we report several objective evaluation metrics, including accuracy (PA$\uparrow$), mean absolute error (PM$\downarrow$) in pitch recognition, and mean absolute error (EM$\downarrow$) in energy recognition. 

It has been known that a minor difference of the discriminability in latent space could hardly be identified in generative tasks, especially considering the subjective nature in the evaluation of the perceptual quality. As such, following the baselines' practice [8,9], we adopt discriminative tasks and quantitative metrics for evaluations instead of comparing Prosody-MAE with other models in speech generation.


> **Q22**: with the regression based style predictor” Citation? Is this FastSpeech’s default f0/energy predictor?

**A22:** Accordingly, we have updated the citation in the revised version of the paper. Thanks for the reviewer's feedback that requests more explanations about the proposed module. The regression-based (simple L1 or L2 losses) style predictor shares a similar architecture with the f0/energy predictor in FastSpeech 2 [17], which is utilized to replace the latent diffusion model for ablation.


> **Q23**: Please add some samples from the model that aren’t in the LJSpeech or LibriTTS corpora so we can hear how it generalizes to unseen text that isn't in the LJSpeech / Librivox style.

**A23:** We use $10$ randomly selected utterances of unseen text in the VCTK dataset that were excluded from the training set for the MOS test. Table shows the experimental results for the out-of-domain text-to-speech synthesis of the unseen text: In summary, we notice that Prosody-TTS achieve high-quality and natural speech synthesis for out-of-domain generalization, indicating that Prosody-TTS can universally generate high-fidelity audio from entirely new texts outside the train set. More speech samples have been attached on demo page for clear comparison.

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer wALL (5/5): Regarding the minor concerns and suggestions

content.title: RE: unseen text samples
content.comment:
> A23: We use  randomly selected utterances of unseen text in the VCTK dataset that were excluded from the training set for the MOS test. Table shows the experimental results for the out-of-domain text-to-speech synthesis of the unseen text: In summary, we notice that Prosody-TTS achieve high-quality and natural speech synthesis for out-of-domain generalization, indicating that Prosody-TTS can universally generate high-fidelity audio from entirely new texts outside the train set. More speech samples have been attached on demo page for clear comparison.

* I don't think that 10 stimuli is enough for an MOS test. I typically run MOS tests with many more (e.g. 1000).
* The "Generalization To Unseen Data (VCTK)" samples on [the demo page](https://prosody-tts.github.io/) are surprising because they roughly clone the voice of the source utterance. If VCTK is unseen in training and these are samples from your model that are only conditioned on text and not the source audio, how could your model produce a voice close to a VCTK speaker when given a VCTK phoneme sequence? 

> "we notice that Prosody-TTS achieve high-quality and natural speech synthesis for out-of-domain generalization, indicating that Prosody-TTS can universally generate high-fidelity audio from entirely new texts outside the train set."

This feels like a strong overstatement given it is based on 20 VCTK samples -- and the demo page only contains 2 of them so I can't hear for myself (the English prosody is quite unnatural to my ear for these 2 samples. I am a native speaker). As I mentioned in my initial review, I think it would make the work stronger if you avoid making overly broad claims such as this and stick to statements of what was actually measured.

content.title: Summary of the response to Reviewer wALL
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestions with effort and time. Your comments helped us better shaping our work. Here, we first summarize our response in addressing your major concerns.

**[Extensive experimental comparison to demonstrate the effectiveness of proposed modules.]**
  
- Per the reviewer's suggestions, we have extensively included the VITS for comparison, suggesting the superiority of Prosody-TTS in capturing and modeling prosodic style patterns (e.g., local rises and falls of the pitch and stress).

- Per the reviewers' suggestions, we introduce a side-by-side AXY subjective test which indicates that raters prefer our model synthesis against baselines in terms of prosody naturalness and expressiveness.  

- To fully justify the diversity of prosodic distribution, we include NDB and JS as quantitative metrics to measure the distribution coverage of speech samples.
 
- To justify the effectiveness and necessity of explicit prosody branch in TTS, we have performed a system comparison based oracle duration. The subjective and objective evaluation indicates the importance of the proposed prosody-MAE in improving the prosody of generated speech, which can be complementary to any existing TTS frameworks.  

**[More detailed explanations and clarification on model design.]**

- As shown in our responses, we acknowledge the reviewer's comments on the duration module but also show the importance of prosody patterns (e.g., local rises and falls of the pitch and stress) by introducing a comparison with rhythm-optimized models. Inheriting the assumption of duration prediction as a fair evaluation, Prosody-TTS keeps the duration module unchanged and focuses on modeling the speaking style appropriate for the given context.

- Per the reviewers' suggestions, we explain the over-smoothing prediction problem in TTS. As the highly multimodal latent representation cannot be well modeled by the simple L1 or L2 losses, they present great challenges in prosody modeling and cause over-smoothed (blurred) predictions.

**[More precise definitions and presentation.]**

- Per the reviewers' suggestions, we provide more precise definitions for hierarchical masking, carefully-crafted information flow, and sub-optimal modeling.

- As shown in our responses, we include the reproducibility statement and revise typos and abbreviations. More speech samples have been attached to the demo page for clear comparison.

We revise the manuscript according to the comments and suggestions of reviewers. We understand that researchers may have their own preference to one over the other based on facts or experiences. We understand that we used a FastSpeech-like duration model, which suffers prosody diversity initially. However, with the proposed Prosody-MAE and the diffusion model based integration to the TTS framework. Most of the issues have been resolved or improved. In the meanwhile, our contribution is more on an effective way of prosody representation learning and its downstream applications. It should be applicable to many multi-speaker expressive TTS frameworks (including VITS). 

We appreciate the reviewer's valuable reviews and believe some misunderstandings are due to our clarity. In this rebuttal phase we have tried to address them carefully, and we sincerely hope that you can consider increasing your score if you find our reply solves your concern. We are always happy to have a further discussion and answer more questions raised by you.

Best regards, Authors

content.title: Response to authors.
content.comment:
Thank you for your extensive responses to my review, and I apologize for my tardy reply. I will respond to each post individually to try and keep things shorter.

> Per the reviewer's suggestions, we have extensively included the VITS for comparison, suggesting the superiority of Prosody-TTS in capturing and modeling prosodic style patterns (e.g., local rises and falls of the pitch and stress).

Apologies but I don't see where this was done? VITS doesn't appear in any results tables or on the demo page I'm looking at. I want to make sure I'm looking at the correct draft. Did you add any experiments with VITS?

> Per the reviewers' suggestions, we introduce a side-by-side AXY subjective test which indicates that raters prefer our model synthesis against baselines in terms of prosody naturalness and expressiveness.

This is a strange use of AXY (A=text, X=baseline, Y=test). I would just call this a AB-7 / CMOS test with text provided. It's a bit of an ill-posed test though. (In Skerry-Ryan 2018 the AXY was used to evaluate prosody transfer, where A was the source utterance to transfer prosody/style from). There are many valid ways of saying a given input text and the right choice of prosody is context dependent. Without the context for these utterances the human evaluators it's difficult to say which of two valid prosodies is the better one.

The sample size of 20 is way too small to be informative, I believe.

> To fully justify the diversity of prosodic distribution, we include NDB and JS as quantitative metrics to measure the distribution coverage of speech samples.

For NDB, how do you cluster the training data? K-means with euclidean distance in log mel spectrogram space? 

As for Jensen-Shannon divergence, please include details of how you computed it. GAN critic trained to optimality? What's the architecture?

> To justify the effectiveness and necessity of explicit prosody branch in TTS, we have performed a system comparison based oracle duration. The subjective and objective evaluation indicates the importance of the proposed prosody-MAE in improving the prosody of generated speech, which can be complementary to any existing TTS frameworks.

I don't understand what the use of oracle durations tells us here -- but it is beside the point I am trying to make. 

Timing is a critical aspect of prosody and it is clear that the prosody latent variable in your diffusion model is not able to influence timing decisions made by the model. I believe you are saying that despite durations being predicted outside of your model, the latent diffusion trained by the prosody-MAE representations seems to be helping with e.g. local rises and falls of pitch. It's great if it does -- however, I don't find this a principled approach to modeling prosody since duration is left out. This is at odds with the language in the manuscript that suggests this is a holistic solution to prosody modeling. For example, the abstract reads "a latent diffusion model to sample and produce diverse patterns within the learned prosodic space. Prosody-TTS achieves high-fidelity speech synthesis with rich and diverse prosodies.". If the latent diffusion model can't affect durations at all, then how can this be diverse?

On testing -- I am surprised by the choice of 20 samples for the AXY and 10 for the unseen VCTK MOS. How many stimuli are used for your other MOS evaluations? I will re-state what I said in my initial review which is that I would never personally compare an MOS number as that's not meaningful for substantially similar systems due to the noise involved in the MOS process (e.g. if the number of stimuli is very low, the evaluator pool non-diverse or biased, etc.). A blind CMOS test is the best way to compare two systems.

> Per the reviewers' suggestions, we provide more precise definitions for hierarchical masking, carefully-crafted information flow, and sub-optimal modeling.

Thanks for this -- I suggest saying "Time-frequency masking" instead of hierarchical. Hierarchical is an overloaded term in my opinion.

I would suggest rewording the terms "carefully crafted information flow" and "sub-optimal modeling" as they are subjective statements, not technical terms.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: Speech consists of both linguistic content and prosody, unlike written text. Hence, it becomes quite a challenge to learn prosodic information in TTS systems. Unlike prior research where ground truth local prosodic attributes are predicted as a means to learn better representation which inevitably leads to worse generated audio quality, the authors propose a self-supervised approach that only requires speech signals (i.e. no ground truth local prosody and transcriptions). Furthermore, to improve the diversity of prosodic information in the generated speech, the authors propose the use of a diffusion model from which different prosodic styles are sampled.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

- Learning prosody in a self-supervised manner opens a path to incorporating bigger datasets which could potentially learn the wide ranges of prosodic attributes. The authors demonstrate the same with a significant impact on the predictability of prosodic attributes of the trained model.
- Improving diversity in the generated prosodic attributes using a generative model is quite novel and improves the perceptual quality of the generated prosody.
- The qualitative examples of the generated speech are quite compelling, both in terms of audio and prosodic quality.
- Most of the design choices and their implications are discussed at length in section 4.3, which is followed by ablation studies on the impact of model components on prosodic modeling.

Weaknesses

- As the model consists of a linguistic encoder, readers would expect to see its impact on the linguistic content of the generated speech. A qualitative/quantitative experiment to measure that could be a good addition to the paper.
- Section 4.2: “Prosody-TTS demonstrates its ability to generate samples with diverse prosodic styles”. Justifying this claim by qualitative inspection of mel-spectrograms of one example is a bit of a stretch. Furthermore, the spectrograms of Prosody-TTS and MetaStyle Speech appear to be quite similar looking, which makes the first claim about the reconstruction of the rich diversity in generated speech not fully justified.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The paper is quite clear, concise, and to the point.
- The quality of the presentation and the experiments is excellent for the most part. There are a couple of overstated claims which could be justified better. See weaknesses.
- The stated contributions are novel and for the most part, are justified by extensive experiments in the paper
- The model looks reproducible from the given information; however a codebase would definitely add value to the paper
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper tackles a challenging problem of generating speech from text with prosodic attributes. It is a well-written paper with extensive quantitative, qualitative, and subjective experiments. My score reflects some of the potentially rectifiable weaknesses mentioned earlier

content.title: Response to Reviewer LdNn
content.comment:
We are grateful for your positive review and valuable feedback, and we hope our response fully resolves your concern.

**[About the linguistic encoder in Prosody-MAE]**


Thanks for the reviewer's feedback that requests more clarification to resolve the misunderstanding on the linguistic encoder. 

The linguistic encoder has never been adopted for TTS training/sampling, which is not attributed to expressive and diverse speech generation, specifically:
- The linguistic encoder is utilized only in Prosody-MAE as part of the information flow design, which ensures the prosody-related attributes (agnostic to linguistic content and speaker identity) can be captured more efficiently in the prosody encoder. 
- The linguistic encoder is discarded and the prosody encoder derives latent prosodic representation during optimizing the TTS model, which is bridged with the TTS conditions (i.e., textual features and target speaker) by the latent diffusion.


**[About the justification of prosody diversity]**

Thanks for the reviewer's suggestion. We agree with the reviewer that the prosody diversity in generated speech is not fully justified via one example of visualization. As such, we employ two common metrics, including the number of Statistically-Different Bins (NDB) and Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD), to explore the diversity of generated mel-spectrograms. Specifically, we 1) cluster the training data into several clusters, and 2) measure how well the generated samples fit into those clusters. For easy comparison, the results are presented in the following table. 




| Method   |    NDB (LJSpeech)    |   JS (LJSpeech)     |   NDB (LibriTTS)    | JS (LibriTTS)     |   
|----------|:-------------:|:-------------:|:-------------:|:-------------:|
|     GT                       |  /          |  /         |   /      |  /        |
|      GT(voc.)             |  19        |   0.02  |   41	|  0.01  |
|      FastSpeech 2    |    45	|   0.05 |   74	|   0.04 |
|  Meta-StyleSpeech |    41	|   0.07 |   58	|   **0.01** |
|      Glow-TTS          |    34	|  0.03 |   61	|   0.03 |
|      Grad-TTS          |    49	|   0.13 |   71	|   0.05 |
|   YourTTS               |    47	|   0.08 |   73	|   0.06 | 
|  Prosody-TTS        |   **30**	|   **0.03**  |   **52**	|   **0.01** |  



In terms of sample diversity, we can see that Prosody-TTS scores the superior NDB with scores of $30$ (LJSpeech) and $52$ (LibriTTS), demonstrating that Prosody-TTS surpasses the baseline models in generating samples with diverse prosody patterns (e.g., local rises and falls of the pitch and stress). Informally, by breaking the generation process into several conditional diffusion steps, generative latent diffusion prevents TTS from learning collapsed prosodic distribution. In contrast, most baseline models learn a mean distribution over their input data which leads to dull speech synthesis with similar patterns.


**[About clarity and reproducibility]**

Thanks for the reviewer's suggestion. We have refined the mentioned instance and included the reproducibility statement in Appendix I in the revised version of the paper. 


Again, we appreciate your positive reviews and sincerely hope our response can fully resolve your concern.

content.title: Response to Authors
content.comment:
Thank you for the responses and pointers to additional results. 
After taking into consideration all the other reviews and the discussions, a few aspects of the paper are still unconvincing:
* I am not able to find the VITS comparison in the paper or the demo
* Even without the VITS comparison, the quality of generated speech (without considering prosody) is significantly more noisy than produced by VITS (https://jaywalnut310.github.io/vits-demo/index.html), even though the MOS values say otherwise, 
* The newly added AXY test with just 20 examples is not comprehensive enough to cover the diversity in human speech.

While this paper is an interesting read, I am not entirely certain of its acceptance in the current state.
